extracted.intended_audience: students (AoPS community; middle and high school) learning to write mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for students on producing clear, precise mathematical proofs, covering fundamental qualities (precision, accuracy, clarity), formal vs informal styles, common proof methods, and practice habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental aspects of a good proof are precision, accuracy, and clarity. A single word can change the intended meaning of a proof, so it is best to be as precise as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exact language; beware that ordinary words (e.g. 'trivial') may have special meanings in mathematical culture. Avoid vague phrasing that could alter the meaning of statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical correctness of each step and correctness of claims made in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each inference follows from prior statements or accepted results; check for hidden assumptions or unjustified leaps. Accuracy is listed as a fundamental aspect alongside precision and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity (clear and complete explanations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make explanations both clear and complete so readers can follow the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the argument logically, state what you are proving, and provide enough detail for the intended audience. For practice: 'Do your best to make your explanations both clear and complete.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish formal vs informal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two different types of proofs: informal and formal. Formal proof is often introduced using a two-column format; informal proofs can be in a wide variety of styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal styles (e.g., two-column) when required by context or instruction; recognize that informal proofs are easier to organize but may lack full rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal proof formats (two-column and higher-level formats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal proof is often introduced using a two-column format, as favored by many geometry teachers. In higher-level mathematics, two methods of formal proof predominate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ the conventional formal structure appropriate to the course or audience (e.g., two-column for school geometry; standard narrative proofs for higher mathematics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by construction (including proof by induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof by construction is a predominant formal method; a common example is proof by induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using construction/induction, explicitly show how the construction or inductive step produces the claimed object/properties and verify base cases and inductive hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof by contradiction is another predominant formal method (in its simplest form requires demonstration of a counterexample).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the assumption to be contradicted, derive a logical contradiction, and conclude the desired result. Ensure the contradiction is explicit and follows logically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of informal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: An informal proof can be in a wide variety of styles but is usually not as neat as a two-column proof. People trained to a university-level of mathematics do not consider so-called 'informal proofs' to be proof of anything at all; instead, they may be regarded as 'heuristics', or teaching tools, at best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use informal proofs for intuition, exposition, or pedagogy, but recognize they may not satisfy rigorous standards for formal validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and peer feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice is essential: use AoPS forums, blogs, and contests to practice writing solutions; read others' solutions and listen to constructive criticisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit solutions, read and compare alternative solutions, accept and act on constructive feedback, and contribute to community resources (AoPSWiki) to improve proof-writing skills over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciation of mathematical culture and terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof writing requires a little appreciation for mathematical culture; for instance, when a mathematician uses the word 'trivial' in a proof, they intend a different meaning to how the word is understood by the wider population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn standard mathematical conventions and usages to avoid misunderstandings; adapt tone and vocabulary to the expectations of the mathematical community and the intended audience.
